newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin named premier, wants EMU talks.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin named premier, wants EMU talks.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac appointed triumphant Socialist leader Lionel Jospin as prime minister on Monday and his party said it would demand assurances that a single European currency would not force more austerity.

"The president offered to appoint me as prime minister. I accepted," Jospin said after meeting Chirac in the Elysee Palace, inaugurating the third period of power-sharing between a rival government and president in France in the past 11 years.

Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande said Jospin, 59, wanted all left-wing parties, including the Communists, to join his government and would reopen talks on a so-called "stability pact" approved by European Union leaders last year to limit their deficits once the single currency takes effect in 1999.
"We want to have assurances the stability pact does not signify new austerity in France," Hollande told Reuters Financial Television.

That could trigger a clash with Germany, which insisted on the pact containing sanctions on countries that exceed the three percent ratio of deficits to gross domestic product as part of the price for abandoning the deutschemark for the euro.
Chirac had a long telephone with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, his main ally in the drive for European integration.
Kohl said on a visit to Paris on May 21 he saw no grounds to renegotiate the terms for the euro, the future currency.

The silver-haired Jospin, defeated by Chirac in a runoff for the presidency in 1995, told reporters that he aimed to form a government "quickly, this week." He takes over formally from defeated premier Alain Juppe on Tuesday at 11 a.m. (0900 GMT).

French financial markets recouped early losses after opening down on news of Sunday's left-wing victory in elections to the National Assembly, where the Socialists will need support from the Communist Party to secure a majority.
The CAC-40 stock market index closed 0.68 percent up after opening 2.7 percent lower. The franc and bonds also recovered from early pressure.
Humiliated by the defeat, Juppe tendered his resignation to his longtime mentor Chirac after their gamble that France would re-elect the ruling centre-right went disastrously awry.

The vote leaves the president a virtual prisoner of a left-wing government, with a shared say in foreign affairs and defence but little influence over domestic and economic policy, just two years into his seven-year term.
Jospin short-circuited official protocol by announcing his own appointment instead of leaving it to the presidency. He said the meeting had taken place in an "excellent" atmosphere.

Final results showed the Socialists and their left-wing allies had won 273 seats in the 577-seat National Assembly and the Communists 38 after Sunday's decisive runoff. The ecologist Greens won eight, their first seats in parliament.

The outgoing centre-right coalition, which had held 464 seats in the outgoing Assembly, crashed to 256. The far-right National Front and an independence campaigner in the French Caribbean island of Martinique won one seat each.

Hollande said the Socialists wanted all forces on the left, including the Communists, to join the government. The Communist Party's national council agreed in principle to enter the cabinet, subject to satisfactory undertakings on policy.
The Greens also voted to join a Jospin administration and said they hoped for an augmented environment ministry and a portfolio covering shorter working hours and women's rights.
The European left rejoiced at the French shift but EU governments pondered what it might mean for economic and monetary union.
"It's too early to say," British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on arrival at an EU ministerial meeting in Luxembourg.

In two previous bouts of "cohabitation" from 1986 to 1988 and from 1993 to 1995, the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand claimed pre-eminence in foreign affairs and left day-to-day domestic policy to centre-right governments.

Monday's change of government stemmed from Chirac's fateful decision on April 21 to call a snap election 10 months early, hoping to win a friendly majority for the rest of his seven-year term until 2002. He said France needed a "new elan" to prepare for a single European currency from 1999.
His pleas fell flat in a country more worried by his broken promises on job creation and lower taxes.

Jospin said after his victory on Sunday that the people had voted for a change of direction in European policy, but at the same time he reaffirmed that the Socialists broadly favoured launching the planned single European currency in 1999.

Hollande reaffirmed the Socialist conditions -- entry of Italy and Spain from the start, creation of a political counterweight to offset the power of a European central bank, creation of an EU pact of solidarity and growth to boost jobs, and the principle that the euro should not be overvalued.

The Socialists have pledged to create 700,000 jobs for young people, half of them in the public sector, over the next three years, and to reduce the working week from 39 hours to 35 over five years without loss of pay.
